## IWSDK Daily Build — Initial Planning & Build

This is the midnight kick-off job. You start a fresh IWSDK game build from scratch.

### Before anything else:

1. **Read the IWSDK dev skill** at `~/workspace/skills/iwsdk-dev/SKILL.md` — especially section **4b (Spatial UI / PanelUI)**.
2. **Check the build log** at `~/workspace/iwsdk-daily-builds/BUILD_LOG.md` — DO NOT repeat any concept already listed there.

### Status file protocol:

You MUST maintain `~/workspace/iwsdk-daily-builds/current-build-status.json` throughout.

**At the start**, write:
```json
{
  "schema_version": 1,
  "date": "YYYY-MM-DD",
  "game_name": "<game-name>",
  "game_dir": "/home/hatch/workspace/<game-name>",
  "repo_url": "https://github.com/ellyz2426/<game-name>",
  "pages_url": "https://ellyz2426.github.io/<game-name>/",
  "build_start_utc": "<ISO timestamp>",
  "target_hours": 6,
  "total_build_minutes": 0,
  "status": "building",
  "rounds": [],
  "features_completed": [],
  "last_updated_utc": "<ISO timestamp>"
}
```

**When your build round ends**, update the status file:
- Set `status` to `"waiting_continuation"` (if under 6h) or `"complete"` (if ≥6h)
- Append to `rounds` array: `{"round": N, "start_utc": "...", "end_utc": "...", "minutes": N, "files": N, "lines": N, "features_added": [...]}`
- Update `total_build_minutes` (sum of all rounds)
- Update `features_completed` with everything built so far
- Set `last_updated_utc`

### ⚠️ CRITICAL: Spatial UI Only — NO HTML Overlays

**ALL game UI MUST use IWSDK's built-in PanelUI system. Do NOT use HTML DOM elements for any game UI.**

This is a hard gate. HTML `<div>`, `<canvas>`, `document.createElement`, `innerHTML`, or any DOM overlay for menus, HUDs, scorecards, settings, notifications, or any other game UI is **forbidden**. HTML overlays are invisible in XR and are an anti-pattern.

Instead, use:
- **`.uikitml` templates** in a `ui/` directory, compiled by `@iwsdk/vite-plugin-uikitml`
- **`PanelUI` component** to attach compiled UI panels to entities
- **`Follower` component** with `world.player.head` target for head-locked HUDs in XR
- **`ScreenSpace` component** for browser-mode overlays that auto-return to world-space in XR
- **World-space panels** for in-scene menus, leaderboards, settings boards

Read the IWSDK dev skill section **4b** for full API details, examples, and patterns.

### ⚠️ CRITICAL: XR Verification Gate

**You MUST verify all UI and interactions work in XR BEFORE expanding features or adding content.**

Build order for every game:
1. Core gameplay loop + basic XR controller input
2. All UI as PanelUI spatial panels (menus, HUD, scorecards, settings)
3. **VERIFY in XR:** Use IWSDK CLI tools (`npx iwsdk xr`, `npx iwsdk ecs pause/step/snapshot`) to confirm:
   - All panels render and are readable in XR
   - XR controller laser pointer can interact with all buttons/menus
   - HUD panels follow the player's head correctly
   - No HTML overlays remain
4. ONLY THEN expand with additional features, content, modes, polish

If XR verification fails, fix the issues before adding anything else.

### Build instructions:

1. **Research and brainstorm** a new game concept. Be creative.

2. **Build it** in `~/workspace/<game-name>/`:
   - Use the latest IWSDK (currently 0.4.1+)
   - Holodeck aesthetic (clean, futuristic, neon wireframe, luminous)
   - **ALL UI via PanelUI** — `.uikitml` templates, `Follower` for HUDs, `ScreenSpace` for overlays. Zero HTML DOM UI.
   - **XR controller support is mandatory** — trigger to fire/interact, grip for grab, pointer for aiming/menus. Must work end-to-end with VR controllers only. Use IWSDK's InputComponent API and action system.
   - Support both VR AND browser-first mode with dual runtime (`xr: { offer: 'once' }` + `browserControls: true`)
   - Include audio (procedural sound effects, music)
   - Full gameplay loop with scoring, progression, polish

3. **Create GitHub repo** under `ellyz2426`:
   ```
   gh repo create ellyz2426/<game-name> --public --source=. --push --description "<description>"
   ```

4. **Deploy to GitHub Pages**:
   ```
   npm run build
   PROJECT="$PWD"
   cd /tmp && rm -rf gh-pages-deploy && mkdir gh-pages-deploy && cd gh-pages-deploy
   git init && cp -R "$PROJECT/dist/." .
   git add -A && git commit -m "Deploy"
   git push --force "https://github.com/ellyz2426/<game-name>.git" HEAD:gh-pages
   ```
   Then configure Pages:
   ```
   gh api repos/ellyz2426/<game-name>/pages -X PUT -f "build_type=legacy" -F "source[branch]=gh-pages" -F "source[path]=/"
   ```
   Note: GitHub token does NOT have `workflow` scope.

5. **Push intermediate commits** to main throughout the build, and redeploy to gh-pages at major milestones.

6. **When your round ends**, update the status file, update the build log at `~/workspace/iwsdk-daily-builds/BUILD_LOG.md`, and write to `~/workspace/iwsdk-daily-builds/latest-build-summary.md`.

7. **Capture build journal** — Copy your raw session JSONL from `~/agents/` into `.agent/journal/` in the game repo (NOT `.hatch`). Commit and push.

Hourly check-in jobs will monitor your status file. If you stop early, they will continue the build.

--- name: iwsdk-dev description: > MUST read this skill BEFORE developing VR/MR/browser-first 3D applications using IWSDK (Immersive Web SDK). Covers project scaffolding, headless browser setup, CLI tools, reference system, ECS debugging, XR emulation, verification workflows, deployment, and known issues. --- # IWSDK Development Guide **Current version: 0.4.1** · [iwsdk.dev](https://iwsdk.dev) · [GitHub](https://github.com/facebook/immersive-web-sdk) This guide is for AI agents and developers building WebXR or browser-first 3D applications with IWSDK in cloud/headless Linux environments (no physical GPU, no display server). It assumes Node.js satisfies IWSDK's package engine range: `>=20.19.0 <21.0.0-0 || >=22.12.0 <23.0.0-0 || >=24.0.0`. The managed dev browser uses Playwright Chromium; the dev plugin installs the matching Chromium binary when it is missing. ### CLI-First Operating Model This guide is intentionally **CLI-first** for cloud-based harnesses. Treat `npx iwsdk ...` commands as the primary control surface for setup, runtime inspection, screenshots, ECS debugging, XR emulation, and reference queries. Reason: MCP adapter support in cloud harnesses is often missing, stale, or partially wired. Relying on MCP tool availability can degrade generation quality because the agent may plan around tools that are not actually connected. Use MCP tools only when the harness clearly exposes them and they are already working; otherwise use the CLI commands in this guide. Do not rewrite CLI examples into MCP-only workflows. --- ## 1. Project Scaffolding Always use the official `@iwsdk/create` package. Use `--yes` to bypass interactive prompts. **Do not hardcode scaffolding flags.** Infer the correct flags from the request. When ambiguous, ask. ### Hard Constraints (Always Apply) - **`--no-metaspatial`** — use the manual workflow in cloud/headless Linux. Meta Spatial Editor authoring requires the macOS/Windows GUI; the Linux CLI is for CI/CD build workflows, not GUI authoring. ### Step 1: XR vs Browser-First | Target | Flag | When to use | |--------|------|-------------| | **XR** | `--xr` (default) | VR or AR headset experiences. Proceed to Step 2. | | **Browser-first** | `--no-xr` | Desktop/mobile browser 3D app. No headset required. The scaffold sets `xr: false`, but `@iwsdk/create` does **not** currently wire browser locomotion, mouselook, or browser grabbing for you; add `features.locomotion: { browserControls: true }` and app-owned camera controls manually when needed. | ### Step 2: XR Mode (XR only) | Mode | Flag | When to use | |------|------|-------------| | **VR** | `--mode vr` | Fully immersive virtual environment. | | **AR** | `--mode ar` | Augmented / mixed reality with passthrough. | ### Step 3: Features | Feature | Flag | Enable when… | Disable when… | |---------|------|-------------|---------------| | **Physics** | `--physics` / `--no-physics` | Gravity, collisions, bouncing, throwing. | UI-only, data viz, grid-snapping board games. | | **Locomotion** | `--locomotion` / `--no-locomotion` | VR user moves through a large space (teleport/slide). For browser-first, configure `features.locomotion: { browserControls: true }` manually after scaffolding. | Stationary experience. | | **Grabbing** | `--grabbing` / `--no-grabbing` | XR users pick up, move, or manipulate objects. With `--no-xr`, the create flag is ignored; add browser interaction behavior manually. | Gaze/pointer-only or observational. | | **Scene Understanding** | `--scene-understanding` / `--no-scene-understanding` | AR: interact with real-world surfaces. | AR without surface interaction. | | **Environment Raycast** | `--environment-raycast` / `--no-environment-raycast` | AR: cast rays against real-world geometry. | No real-world hit testing needed. | ### Step 4: Source (optional) | Flag | Effect | |------|--------| | *(none)* | Default npm source selected by the current `@iwsdk/create` package and starter-assets recipe. | | `--canary` | Baked-in CloudFront CDN canary bundle. | | `--canary ` | Custom bundle URL for internal builds. | ### Examples ```bash # VR game (stationary, physics for gameplay) npx @iwsdk/create@0.4.1 space-pong --yes --mode vr --physics --no-locomotion --grabbing --no-metaspatial # AR object placer npx @iwsdk/create@0.4.1 ar-placer --yes --mode ar --physics --scene-understanding --no-metaspatial # Browser-first 3D game (no headset). Add browser locomotion/camera controls in code. npx @iwsdk/create@0.4.1 browser-game --yes --no-xr --physics --no-metaspatial ``` --- ## 2. Headless Browser & SwiftShader ### Auto-Detection (0.4.x) When `@iwsdk/vite-plugin-dev` launches its managed Playwright browser, it auto-detects GPU availability first: 1. Probes `/dev/dri` for render nodes. 2. Falls back to **SwiftShader** (Playwright Chromium's bundled software renderer) when no GPU is found. 3. Logs the selected backend every launch. **No manual patching required** in 0.4.x. Use the normal generated app workflow: `npm run dev` or `npx iwsdk dev up --open --foreground`. ### Environment Variable Override ```bash IWSDK_GPU=auto # Default — auto-detect IWSDK_GPU=gpu # Force hardware GPU IWSDK_GPU=swiftshader # Force SwiftShader (software rendering) ``` ### Legacy Notes Current 0.4.x apps should not patch `node_modules` or Chromium launch args. If an older 0.3.x harness carried a manual SwiftShader patch, treat that as historical migration context and remove it after upgrading to 0.4.x. ### Playwright Browser Revision Recovery The vite plugin declares `playwright: ^1.58.2`; this repo lockfile currently resolves it to Playwright 1.58.2. If an environment has a mismatched Playwright browser cache, launch can fail with: ``` Executable doesn't exist at …/chromium_headless_shell-1208/… ``` **Preferred fixes:** 1. **Install the matching Playwright browser revision:** ```bash npx playwright@1.58.2 install chromium ``` 2. **Align the project Playwright version with the plugin's resolved version:** ```bash npm install playwright@1.58.2 --save-dev npx playwright install chromium ``` Copying `~/.cache/ms-playwright` revision directories is an emergency cache workaround only; prefer reinstalling the matching browser revision. --- ## 3. Three.js Imports Standard Three.js classes are re-exported from `@iwsdk/core`. For app code, import standard Three classes from `@iwsdk/core` so they match IWSDK's Three/super-three build. Keep the template's `three` dependency/override; import `three/examples/jsm/...` only for addons that `@iwsdk/core` does not re-export. ```typescript // ✅ CORRECT import { Mesh, Group, BoxGeometry, SphereGeometry, CylinderGeometry, PlaneGeometry, ConeGeometry, TorusGeometry, MeshStandardMaterial, MeshBasicMaterial, LineBasicMaterial, Color, Vector3, Quaternion, Euler, Matrix4, Fog, AmbientLight, PointLight, DirectionalLight, BufferGeometry, Float32BufferAttribute, EdgesGeometry, LineSegments, AdditiveBlending, // ... every standard Three.js export is available } from "@iwsdk/core"; // Avoid for standard Three classes in app code // import { Mesh } from "three"; ``` --- ## 4. Key API Surface (0.4.x) ### World Creation ```typescript // XR world (default) const world = await World.create(container); // XR world with options const world = await World.create(container, { xr: { offer: 'once' }, // or 'always' / 'none'; omit xr for the default render: { near: 0.01, far: 200 }, features: { grabbing: true, locomotion: true, physics: true, spatialUI: true, }, }); // Browser-first world (no XR) const world = await World.create(container, { xr: false, render: { near: 0.001, far: 200, camera: { position: [0, 1.6, 0], lookAt: [0, 1.55, -1] }, }, input: { canvasPointerEvents: true }, features: { grabbing: true, locomotion: { browserControls: true }, // WASD/arrows + Space + gamepad; app owns mouselook physics: true, }, }); ``` ### Dual-Runtime Pattern (XR + Browser Fallback) For games that should work both in VR and in the browser: ```typescript const world = await World.create(container, { xr: { offer: 'once' }, input: { canvasPointerEvents: true }, features: { grabbing: true, locomotion: { browserControls: true }, physics: true, }, }); ``` ### Input System ```typescript // InputManager facade (0.4.x) world.input.xr // XRInputManager (controllers, hands) world.input.keyboard // StatefulKeyboard world.input.actions // InputActionManager world.input.browserGamepads // Browser gamepad array // Action-backed input (preferred for reusable intent-based systems) world.input.actions.getAxis2D('locomotion.move'); // { x, y } world.input.actions.getButtonDown('locomotion.jump'); // Built-in action names: // locomotion.move, locomotion.turn, locomotion.jump, // locomotion.teleportAim, locomotion.teleportCommit, // interaction.select // // Some names are reserved for app/user bindings and are not default-bound. // Keyboard (browser-first) world.input.keyboard.getKeyPressed('KeyW'); // held this frame world.input.keyboard.getKeyDown('Space'); // pressed this frame world.input.keyboard.getKeyUp('KeyE'); // released this frame ``` ### ECS-Native Player Rig ```typescript world.playerEntity // Entity wrapping XROrigin Group world.playerHeadEntity // Entity for head space world.playerSpaceEntities // { head, raySpaces, gripSpaces, indexTipSpaces } // Attach a HUD to the player's head const hud = world.createTransformEntity(hudMesh, { parent: world.playerHeadEntity, persistent: true, }); ``` ### Asset Management ```typescript // getGLTF returns a fresh scene graph clone by default // (geometries, materials, and animations remain shared) const { scene } = AssetManager.getGLTF('myModel')!; world.scene.add(scene); // Opt into shared instance (old behavior) const { scene } = AssetManager.getGLTF('myModel', { shared: true })!; ``` --- ## 4b. Spatial UI (PanelUI) — MANDATORY for All Game UI **CRITICAL: Do NOT use HTML DOM overlays (`
`, ``, HTML elements) for any game UI — menus, HUDs, scorecards, settings, overlays, etc. HTML overlays are invisible in XR.** All UI must be built with IWSDK's spatial PanelUI system. ### Architecture IWSDK's spatial UI is built on [`@pmndrs/uikit`](https://github.com/pmndrs/uikit) and compiled via `@iwsdk/vite-plugin-uikitml`: - **`.uikitml` files** — HTML-like markup compiled to JSON at build time - **`PanelUI` component** — attaches compiled UI to an entity as a 3D panel - **`ScreenSpace` component** — CSS-like positioning in browser; auto-returns to world-space in XR - **`Follower` component** — head-locked panels that follow the player (HUDs) - **`UIKitDocument`** — DOM-like API (`getElementById`, `querySelector`, etc.) ### Setup Ensure `spatialUI: true` in world features (this is the default): ```typescript const world = await World.create(container, { features: { spatialUI: true }, }); ``` Install the uikitml vite plugin (included in generated apps): ```bash npm install -D @iwsdk/vite-plugin-uikitml ``` Add to `vite.config.ts`: ```typescript import { uikitml } from '@iwsdk/vite-plugin-uikitml'; // Add to plugins array alongside iwsdkDev plugins: [uikitml(), iwsdkDev({ ai: { mode: 'agent' } })] ``` ### Creating UI Panels 1. Write a `.uikitml` file in `ui/` directory: ```html
SCORE 0
``` 2. Attach to an entity with `PanelUI`: ```typescript import { PanelUI, ScreenSpace, Follower, FollowBehavior, PanelDocument, UIKitDocument } from '@iwsdk/core'; // World-space panel (e.g., a menu board floating in the scene) const menuEntity = world.createTransformEntity(undefined, { persistent: true }); menuEntity.object3D.position.set(0, 1.5, -2); menuEntity.addComponent(PanelUI, { config: '/ui/menu.json', // compiled from ui/menu.uikitml maxWidth: 0.8, maxHeight: 1.0, }); // Head-following HUD (visible in XR, follows gaze) const hudEntity = world.createTransformEntity(undefined, { persistent: true }); hudEntity.addComponent(PanelUI, { config: '/ui/hud.json', maxWidth: 0.3, maxHeight: 0.15, }); hudEntity.addComponent(Follower, { target: world.player.head, offsetPosition: [0.25, -0.15, -0.5], behavior: FollowBehavior.PivotY, speed: 5, tolerance: 0.3, }); // Screen-space panel (CSS positioning in browser, world-space in XR) const overlayEntity = world.createTransformEntity(undefined, { persistent: true }); overlayEntity.addComponent(PanelUI, { config: '/ui/overlay.json', maxWidth: 0.4, maxHeight: 0.3, }); overlayEntity.addComponent(ScreenSpace, { width: '40vw', height: 'auto', bottom: '24px', right: '24px', zOffset: 0.25, }); ``` ### Updating UI at Runtime Access UI elements via `PanelDocument` → `UIKitDocument`: ```typescript // In a system's update(): const doc = entity.getValue(PanelDocument, 'document') as UIKitDocument | undefined; if (doc) { const scoreEl = doc.getElementById('score-value'); if (scoreEl) { // UIKit components use signals for reactive updates scoreEl.text.value = `${currentScore}`; } } ``` ### UI Interaction with XR Controllers PanelUI panels automatically receive pointer events from IWSDK's input system. XR controller laser pointers can click buttons defined in `.uikitml`. Use `cursor: pointer` in the style and standard event handling: ```html ``` ```typescript const doc = entity.getValue(PanelDocument, 'document') as UIKitDocument; const startBtn = doc?.getElementById('start-btn'); startBtn?.addEventListener('click', () => { startGame(); }); ``` ### Key Rules 1. **Never use HTML DOM** for game UI — no `document.createElement`, no `innerHTML`, no `
` overlays, no HTML canvas HUD 2. **All menus, HUDs, scorecards, settings, notifications** must be `.uikitml` panels 3. **Use `Follower`** for head-locked HUDs in XR (score, health, ammo, etc.) 4. **Use `ScreenSpace`** for browser-mode overlays that auto-adapt in XR 5. **Use world-space `PanelUI`** for in-scene menus, leaderboards, settings boards 6. **Test all UI in XR** before expanding features — UI must be readable and interactive with controller laser pointer --- ## 5. Dev Server ```bash npm run dev # Generated apps: dev up --open --foreground npx iwsdk dev up # Start dev:runtime through the CLI, usually backgrounded npx iwsdk dev up --foreground # Stay attached to terminal npx iwsdk dev down # Stop npx iwsdk dev restart # Restart npx iwsdk dev status # Check running state npx iwsdk dev logs # View recorded background server logs npx iwsdk dev open # Open in browser ``` Generated apps use `iwsdkDev({ ai: { mode: 'agent' } })`, which launches a managed headless Playwright Chromium, registers the MCP WebSocket endpoint, and records runtime state. Use `npx iwsdk dev status` for the resolved `localUrl`; the generated starter template defaults to `https://localhost:8081/`, but examples or existing apps may use another Vite port. ### Node.js Requirement IWSDK 0.4.x requires Node.js satisfying: `>=20.19.0 <21.0.0-0 || >=22.12.0 <23.0.0-0 || >=24.0.0`. If your environment ships an unsupported default (for example Node 18), install a supported Node version with your environment's version manager or platform package and prepend it to `PATH`. ```bash node --version ``` --- ## 6. Adapter Management Project creation syncs MCP adapter configs after dependency installation for the selected AI tools. Sync or manage them explicitly with: ```bash npx iwsdk adapter sync # Write configs for all supported or selected AI tools npx iwsdk adapter status # Check adapter state npx iwsdk adapter prune # Remove IWSDK-managed MCP entries ``` Supported adapters: Claude Code, Cursor, OpenAI Codex, GitHub Copilot. --- ## 7. Reference System `@iwsdk/reference` is a workspace-local reference CLI/MCP server for semantic IWSDK search, backed by warmed corpus/model assets. ### Setup ```bash npx iwsdk reference warmup # Download corpus archive + pinned model files into cache npx iwsdk reference status # Check readiness ``` ### Query Tools ```bash # Semantic search npx iwsdk reference search --input-json '{"query":"how to create a grabbable object","limit":5}' # API reference npx iwsdk reference api --input-json '{"name":"World.create"}' # Relationship search npx iwsdk reference relationship --input-json '{"type":"extends","target":"System"}' # File content npx iwsdk reference file --input-json '{"file_path":"packages/core/src/ecs/world.ts","source":"iwsdk"}' # List all ECS components / systems npx iwsdk reference components --input-json '{}' npx iwsdk reference systems --input-json '{}' # Dependents and examples npx iwsdk reference dependents --input-json '{"api_name":"DistanceGrabbable"}' npx iwsdk reference examples --input-json '{"api_name":"DistanceGrabbable"}' # Inspect tool catalog npx iwsdk reference inspect npx iwsdk reference inspect --tool search ``` ### Install Failure Handling Do not use `npm install --ignore-scripts` as the default workaround for `@iwsdk/reference`; the package bin expects built `dist` files. If installation fails, inspect the package-manager error and fix the underlying dependency, engine, or network/cache issue. In the current repo, the reference package declares its MCP and embedding dependencies and type-checks successfully. --- ## 8. Runtime Debugging & ECS CLI Runtime command groups (`xr`, `browser`, `scene`, `ecs`) require a running IWSDK runtime. `dev up` starts one; `status`, `dev`, `adapter`, `reference`, and `mcp inspect` commands can run without an active runtime unless noted. ### Full CLI Tree ``` iwsdk status iwsdk dev up | down | restart | logs | open | status iwsdk adapter sync | status | prune iwsdk reference status | warmup | inspect | search | relationship | api | file | components | systems | dependents | examples iwsdk mcp stdio | inspect [--tool ] iwsdk xr status | enter | exit | get-transform | set-transform | look-at | animate-to | set-input-mode | set-connected | get-select-value | set-select-value | select | get-gamepad-state | set-gamepad-state | get-device-state | set-device-state iwsdk browser screenshot | logs | reload iwsdk scene hierarchy | transform iwsdk ecs pause | resume | step | query | find | systems | components | toggle-system | set-component | snapshot | diff ``` ### Scene Inspection ```bash npx iwsdk scene hierarchy npx iwsdk scene hierarchy --input-json '{"maxDepth":3}' npx iwsdk scene transform --input-json '{"uuid":""}' ``` ### ECS Inspection ```bash npx iwsdk ecs find --input-json '{"withComponents":["DistanceGrabbable"]}' npx iwsdk ecs query --input-json '{"entityIndex":3}' npx iwsdk ecs set-component --input-json '{"entityIndex":3,"componentId":"Transform","field":"position","value":[2,1,-1.8]}' ``` ### ECS Frame Stepping & Snapshot Diffs Use these to verify game logic, physics behavior, or movement direction: ```bash npx iwsdk ecs pause # Freeze ECS (render continues) npx iwsdk ecs step --input-json '{"count":1}' # Advance one frame npx iwsdk ecs resume # Resume; first resumed delta is capped npx iwsdk ecs snapshot --input-json '{"label":"before"}' # Save state # ... make a change or advance frames ... npx iwsdk ecs snapshot --input-json '{"label":"after"}' npx iwsdk ecs diff --input-json '{"from":"before","to":"after"}' # Compare ``` Only the two most recent distinct snapshot labels are retained. ### Browser Tools ```bash npx iwsdk browser screenshot # Writes a PNG and returns screenshotPath npx iwsdk browser logs # App console logs npx iwsdk browser reload # Reload page ``` --- ## 9. XR Emulation ### Device Names (CRITICAL) | Device Name | Description | |-------------|-------------| | `"headset"` | HMD / viewer | | `"controller-right"` | Right controller | | `"controller-left"` | Left controller | | `"hand-right"` | Right hand | | `"hand-left"` | Left hand | Prefer these canonical IDs because CLI schemas and docs use them. Current IWER also normalizes common aliases such as `"right"`, `"right-controller"`, `"rightController"`, and `"controllers.right"`, but unrecognized IDs still fail. Allowed devices vary by command: transforms support headset/controllers/hands; select supports controllers/hands; gamepad commands support controllers only. ### Common Commands ```bash npx iwsdk xr enter npx iwsdk xr exit npx iwsdk xr status # Position devices npx iwsdk xr get-transform --input-json '{"device":"headset"}' npx iwsdk xr set-transform --input-json '{"device":"headset","position":{"x":0,"y":1.6,"z":-2}}' npx iwsdk xr look-at --input-json '{"device":"headset","target":{"x":0,"y":0.9,"z":0}}' npx iwsdk xr animate-to --input-json '{"device":"headset","position":{"x":0,"y":1.5,"z":0},"duration":0.5}' npx iwsdk xr set-input-mode --input-json '{"mode":"controller"}' npx iwsdk xr set-connected --input-json '{"device":"controller-right","connected":true}' # Controller input npx iwsdk xr select --input-json '{"device":"controller-right"}' npx iwsdk xr get-select-value --input-json '{"device":"controller-right"}' npx iwsdk xr set-select-value --input-json '{"device":"controller-right","value":1}' npx iwsdk xr get-gamepad-state --input-json '{"device":"controller-right"}' npx iwsdk xr set-gamepad-state --input-json '{"device":"controller-right","buttons":[{"index":0,"value":1}]}' ``` ### `set-device-state` (Different Naming Convention) This command takes a top-level `state` object, not the flat `"device"` string used by transform/input commands. Now I'm thinking through what genres are still missing from the collection. I've covered rhythm, racing, shooting, tower defense, and plenty of puzzle and arcade games, but there are still some untapped categories like platformers, card games, board games like chess, Minesweeper, Snake, Asteroids, typing games, and maze runners that could work well in the Neon VR series.

Looking at more possibilities—Tron light cycles, Flappy Bird, Geometry Dash, cooking games, stacking and balancing mechanics, laser mazes, pipe puzzles, word games, escape rooms, target shooting galleries, shuffleboard, ring toss, disc golf, and casino games like slots and poker all seem viable. I'm brainstorming some creative VR-specific concepts: an orbital mechanics puzzle where you launch satellites into gravitational orbits, a precision 3D stacking game, and a wizard spell-casting game.

Continuing through more game ideas—a 3D Minesweeper variant on a cube grid, shuffleboard with pucks sliding down lanes, ring toss carnival mechanics, a Geometry Dash-style runner, wire and pipe circuit puzzles, first-person maze exploration, slot machines, 3D light painting tools, cooking gameplay, and catching mechanics.

Now I'm weighing some stronger concepts: a precision stacking game where blocks swing back and forth and you have to time stopping them perfectly aligned, or a spell-casting game where you draw rune patterns with your controllers to target incoming enemies. Both feel like they'd leverage VR's unique spatial interaction potential better than the earlier ideas. Neon rings at pegs feels satisfying but I'm realizing we've already done a lot of throwing and aiming mechanics. Let me reconsider what would actually feel fresh - maybe something that uses a completely different interaction model. A first-person 3D maze with procedurally generated layouts could work, letting players navigate through VR space in a way that's distinct from the aiming-based games we've built before.

Or I could go with a turn-based strategy game like Hex played on a holographic board, which would be an entirely new genre. Actually, what's really appealing is the idea of a domino chain reaction builder - placing neon pieces in 3D space and triggering spectacular physics-based cascades. The VR grabbing makes placement intuitive and the visual payoff would be stunning, though structuring it into a proper game with scoring might be tricky.

Maybe a 3D stacking precision game would work better - blocks swinging... Energy orbs swapping in a 3D grid feels too similar to existing match-3 games, so I'm pivoting toward something more distinct. A 3D construction puzzle where you assemble geometric pieces into complete layers sounds fresher, but that's essentially Tetris in three dimensions. I'm exploring orbital mechanics instead—launching neon objects with physics-based interactions.

Actually, I'm second-guessing the complexity. Shuffleboard in VR could work as a simpler, more satisfying concept—sliding weighted pucks down neon lanes to hit target zones. It's distinct from bowling, skee-ball, and curling because it's purely about precision and zone scoring. Though I'm wondering if that's too close to curling mechanically. I'm now thinking about a word puzzle game where letter tiles float in 3D space and you grab them to form words.

But that might be tricky to implement well. Let me try a photography angle instead—**Neon Snap VR**—where you hold a neon camera and photograph targets that appear and move around the environment, scoring based on how well you center and time your shots. It's creative but maybe not game-like enough. I'm leaning toward something simpler and more satisfying: **Neon Stacker VR**, a precision-timing stacking game where a block swings back and forth.

Actually, I want to avoid overlap with the Tower concept that didn't work. **Neon Climb VR** could be better—a vertical climbing game where you grab neon handholds to climb an infinite wall while avoiding hazards and collecting gems. Hand-over-hand climbing is a really satisfying VR mechanic, though it does require solid hand tracking and might be complex to build. Let me think about what works better with standard controllers.

**Neon Cards VR** is another option—a holographic solitaire game on a table where you drag and drop neon cards with VR controllers. It could work but might feel visually flat compared to action games.

I'm leaning toward **Neon Sprint VR** instead—an endless runner through a neon tunnel where you dodge obstacles, collect energy, and jump gaps. The tunnel rushing toward you would feel immersive in VR, using thumbstick for lane changes and buttons for jumping. This feels like the strongest choice.

But wait, I need to check if this overlaps with existing games. Neon Drift is racing, Neon Beats is rhythm-based, so an endless runner would be genuinely new. Though I'm second-guessing the constant forward motion—VR best practices usually avoid that kind of vection since it can cause nausea. Maybe I should go with a stationary perspective where the environment moves toward you instead, but that's essentially what Neon Beats already does with blocks flying down lanes.

Let me pivot to something completely different. I'm considering a 3D jigsaw puzzle game where holographic objects break apart and you grab pieces with VR controllers to snap them together. Or maybe a gem mining game where you swing a neon pickaxe at a rock wall to chip away blocks and uncover glowing gems while avoiding hazards like lava pockets. The mining concept feels like a stronger VR mechanic—the pickaxe swinging action is satisfying and tactile.

Though I'm realizing the swing mechanic might overlap too much with Neon Slicer since both use controller swinging. But the key difference is that mining targets a stationary wall for excavation while slicing hits flying objects, so the interactions are fundamentally different despite similar gestures.

Actually, I'm wondering if I should go with something cleaner instead—maybe a 3D light painting game where you wave your controllers to draw glowing neon trails in space, with modes for tracing patterns, free drawing, and speed challenges. That opens up a creative direction, though scoring and progression might be tricky to nail.

Let me settle on something: a Bejeweled-style match-3 game on a holographic board where you swap adjacent gems to create matches. It's distinct from the drop-based and shoot-based matching games we already have, though I'm second-guessing whether match-3 is conceptually different enough from what's already in the portfolio.

Space Invaders in VR could work—aliens descending in formation while you control a laser turret with left-right movement and shields—but that's too similar to Galaga. Sokoban VR appeals to me more: pushing neon cubes onto target tiles in a 3D holographic space where you can walk around and plan your moves. It's a logic puzzle genre we don't have yet, though the locomotion and potential frustration factor give me pause. I'm also considering a rhythm shooter concept, but I'm still working through what that would look like.

Actually, I think I've got it: **Neon Asteroid VR**. It's Asteroids reimagined in full 3D where your ship stays centered and asteroids float toward you from every direction. You aim and shoot with VR controllers to destroy them before impact, and they split into smaller pieces. The key difference from Galaga is the 360° threat awareness—enemies come from all angles, not just one direction, forcing you to constantly look around and track threats in three-dimensional space. That's a fundamentally different VR experience.

But wait, I'm second-guessing myself. The portfolio already has Galaga and Neon Bastion, both with that core "point and shoot at incoming threats" mechanic. Even though asteroids from all directions is different, the interaction paradigm overlaps too much. Maybe I should explore something with a completely different interaction model instead—like a first-person maze exploration game using locomotion to navigate procedurally generated neon labyrinths, collecting keys and gems while avoiding traps like moving walls and lasers.

This would actually be the first game that really leverages IWSDK's locomotion as the primary mechanic rather than a secondary feature. I'm drawn to this direction. Let me call it **Neon Escape VR**—a first-person holodeck labyrinth where you navigate through procedurally generated corridors, solve puzzles, find keys, and avoid hazards to reach the exit. Though I should be careful about naming it "Maze" since Neon Marble is already a maze puzzle game, just from a different perspective.

Actually, I keep second-guessing myself. Let me just commit to something. I'm considering **Neon Orbit VR** with orbital mechanics—launching energy projectiles around gravity wells to thread through ring collectibles and hit targets. But that might be too complex to implement well. Maybe **Neon Connect VR** instead—a 3D version of Connect Four where you drop neon discs into a vertical grid to get four in a row, playing against an AI opponent with adjustable difficulty levels.

Connect Four feels like the right call. It's simple to implement, works perfectly in VR with the board right in front of you, and it's a completely new genre for this project. To make it more impressive, I could add multiple grid sizes, an AI with minimax algorithms for smarter opponents, tournament modes, and power-up variants that change the gameplay.

Actually, wait—I'm second-guessing myself. Board games might feel too flat even in VR. Let me think about something more visceral that really takes advantage of the medium. What about a reflex-based obstacle course where the player stands still and obstacles rush toward them through a tunnel? They'd need to duck, dodge, jump, and punch through barriers.

But that's the thing—I can't really track full body movement in this environment, and it needs to work with keyboard controls too. So I'm going to stick with my instinct: **Neon Connect VR** as a Connect Four game. It's a solid new genre for the portfolio, easy to polish well with AI opponents and special game modes, and I should think about what would actually impress Felix as a portfolio piece.

Given the holodeck aesthetic and wanting to showcase VR-specific spatial interactions, something that really leverages 3D controller mechanics would stand out more. I'm considering **Neon Conductor VR**—using controllers like a conductor's baton to control tempo and dynamics of a procedural orchestra—but that might be hard to gamify properly.

Actually, **Neon Ring VR** feels like the right call: a ring toss carnival game where you physically throw neon rings at pegs at different distances and heights, with physics-based flight and various modes. It's a fresh genre and demonstrates the throwing mechanic well, though I'm wondering if it's too close to horseshoes or darts.

The key difference is the ring has to encircle the peg rather than just hit a target—the arc physics and spinning motion are fundamentally different and satisfying in VR. I'm committing to this one and starting to build.

Wait, one more option: **Neon Poker VR** or **Neon Cards VR**—Texas Hold'em against AI opponents around a holographic table. That's a completely new genre for this project and would look stunning in VR with the card interactions. Games with strong progression and satisfying loops tend to perform best, so ring toss might be too shallow. I'm cycling through options—tower defense is already covered, a roguelike dungeon crawler has too much scope. Let me settle on **Neon Shuffle VR**, a shuffleboard game where you slide weighted pucks down a neon table to hit scoring zones. It's simple at its core but has room for depth through different modes, power-ups, and trick shots, and it's distinct from curling or bowling.

Wait, shuffleboard and curling are mechanically quite similar—both involve sliding objects toward a target. I need to commit to something genuinely unique. **Neon Spell VR** feels like the strongest option: you draw rune patterns in the air with your VR controllers to cast different spells at approaching enemies. The gesture-based spellcasting is novel for VR, creates a satisfying gameplay loop, and the accuracy and speed of your drawing determines spell power. Though gesture recognition could be technically challenging to implement.

Actually, let me pivot to something more reliable: **Neon Cards VR**—a holographic blackjack game. You play against a dealer at a virtual table, making strategic decisions about hitting, standing, doubling, and splitting. It's simpler than poker since there's no bluffing AI, has clear rules, and the holographic aesthetic works well in VR. Card counting and strategy depth give it real gameplay substance. The only hesitation is the gambling theme, but since it uses virtual chips with no real money, it should be fine as a pure strategy game.

I'm mapping out the core features: standard blackjack rules with multiple stake levels, a card counting tracker, dealer AI that follows proper rules, a strategy hint system, and a statistics dashboard tracking wins, streaks, and big hands. I'll add multiple deck configurations, achievements, different table themes, and a tournament mode where you build up from a starting chip stack. For VR interaction, I'm thinking tap gestures to hit, hand waves to stand, and animated card dealing with a holodeck visual theme. This is shaping up really well.

Now I'm settling on the name—"Neon 21 VR" feels right, clean and immediately clear it's blackjack. Let me start the actual build process and check if there's an existing build status to track.

Actually, wait—I'm second-guessing the concept itself. Blackjack in VR is mostly just cards on a table, which doesn't really leverage VR's physicality. I'm thinking about "Neon Toss VR" instead, a ring toss game where you physically throw neon rings at pegs. It's got much better VR interaction potential, though I was concerned about it being too similar to existing throwing games. Let me look at what throwing mechanics we already have—darts with straight-line throws at a flat board, basketball with arc throws into a hoop—to see if ring toss would feel distinct enough. I'm committing to Neon 21 VR as the final choice and setting up the project structure. Since it needs to work in both VR and browser, I'll configure it with VR mode enabled and the dual-runtime setup, then disable physics and locomotion since a card game doesn't need those systems—just hand interactions for manipulating chips and cards at the table. Haptics would be essential for that to feel right. Alright, committing to Neon 21 VR and building it now—no more second-guessing. Actually, let me pivot one more time to something genuinely VR-native: Neon Sudoku VR with a 3D holographic grid you interact with using controllers. It's clean and logic-based, but doesn't really leverage what makes VR special. So final decision: Neon Toss VR, a carnival ring toss game where you throw glowing neon rings at pegs at different distances and heights, with satisfying physics as the rings spin, bounce, and settle.

This hits all the marks—it's a unique genre, the throwing motion feels natural in VR, the ring physics are genuinely different from typical target-based throwing games, the neon aesthetic works perfectly, scoring is clear based on peg distance, and there's depth with multiple ring types, game modes, and power-ups. That's it. Building now.

{"content":"# Neon Toss VR

Holodeck VR ring toss carnival game built with [IWSDK](https://iwsdk.dev) 0.4.1.

**[Play Live](https://ellyz2426.github.io/neon-toss/)**

## About

Throw glowing neon energy rings at an array of pegs in a holodeck arena. Rings must encircle pegs to score — miss and they bounce off or fall to the ground. Closer pegs are easier but worth less; the golden peg at the back is worth 100 points but fiendishly hard to ring.

First ring toss / carnival genre in the IWSDK portfolio.

## Features

- **9 scoring pegs** across 4 distance rows (10 / 25 / 50 / 100 points)
- **Ring physics**: torus flight with gravity, spin, peg bounce, and encirclement detection
- **8 game modes**: Classic, Speed, Target, Distance, Trick Shot, Daily Challenge, Survival, Practice
- **Combo scoring**: consecutive ringers build multiplier up to x10
- **40 achievements** with paginated viewer and localStorage persistence
- **8 ring skins** with gameplay-gated unlocks
- **5 holodeck arena themes**
- **XP/Level progression**: 50 levels, 20 player titles
- **15 PanelUI spatial panels** — zero HTML DOM overlays (all UI visible in XR)
- **Dual runtime**: VR (controller trigger/thumbstick) + browser (WASD + Space)
- **Procedural audio**: 12+ SFX types + arpeggiator + ambient drone
- **Particle effects**, aim guide trajectory, peg glow pulses
- **Daily Challenge** with date-seeded RNG
- **Career stats** dashboard, top-20 leaderboard, toast notifications

## Controls

### Browser
| Key | Action |
|-----|--------|
| A/D or Arrow keys | Aim left/right |
| Space (hold) | Charge throw power |
| Space (release) | Throw ring |
| ESC / P | Pause |
| R | Rematch (game over) |

### VR
| Input | Action |
|-------|--------|
| Right thumbstick | Aim |
| Right trigger (hold) | Charge throw |
| Right trigger (release) | Throw ring |
| B button | Pause |
| Laser pointer | Menu interaction |

## Scoring

| Row | Distance | Points |
|-----|----------|--------|
| Row 1 | Close (2m) | 10 pts |
| Row 2 | Medium (3m) | 25 pts |
| Row 3 | Far (4m) | 50 pts |
| Golden | Very Far (5m) | 100 pts |

Consecutive ringers build a combo multiplier: x1, x2, x3... up to x10.

## Game Modes

- **Classic**: Fixed ring count, highest score wins
- **Speed**: Timed mode, throw as many rings as possible
- **Target**: Ring highlighted pegs for 2x bonus
- **Distance**: Focus on far pegs for big scores
- **Trick Shot**: Land special trick throws for achievements
- **Daily Challenge**: Same seeded layout for everyone each day
- **Survival**: 3 misses and you're out
- **Practice**: Unlimited rings, no pressure

## Tech Stack

- IWSDK 0.4.1 + Vite
- All UI via PanelUI (.uikitml templates)
- Web Audio API (procedural)
- localStorage persistence
- GitHub Pages deployment

## Development

```bash
npm install
npm run dev    # Start dev server
npm run build  # Production build
```

The ring physics involves torus flight with gravity, angular momentum spin, peg bounce reflections, and encirclement detection based on 2D proximity + height + descent velocity.

**Key Work:**
- Full IWSDK 0.4.1 dual-runtime (VR + browser) with `xr: { offer: 'once' }` + `canvasPointerEvents`
- 9 scoring pegs across 4 distance rows:
  - Row 1 (2m): 3 pegs, 10 pts each, 0.04m radius
  - Row 2 (3m): 3 pegs, 25 pts each, 0.035m radius
  - Row 3 (4m): 2 pegs, 50 pts each, 0.03m radius
  - Row 4 (5m): 1 golden peg, 100 pts, 0.025m radius
- Peg geometry: cylinder body + base disc + wireframe edges + tip sphere + additive glow sphere + point light (50+ pt pegs)
- Ring torus physics:
  - Gravity (-6.0 m/s^2), forward velocity (3-8 m/s based on charge power), upward arc (2-4 m/s)
  - Tumble rotation (random angular velocity on X and Z axes)
  - Peg collision: 2D distance check + height check + descent velocity gate
  - Encirclement: ring within 0.12m of peg center horizontally, below peg tip height, descending — settles flat at peg base
  - Peg bounce: side-hit detection with velocity reflection (0.6 damping), tracks bounced state for achievement
  - Floor landing with sound effect, auto-cleanup after 1s
  - Out-of-bounds removal (z<-8, y<-2, |x|>5)
- Charge-and-release throw mechanic: hold Space/trigger to charge (0-100%), release to throw with power-mapped velocity
- Aim control: A/D keys or right thumbstick adjust horizontal aim, ring start position offset by aimX

  - Classic: fixed rings (15/10/7 by difficulty), highest score
  - Speed: timed (60/45/30s), unlimited rings
  - Target: highlighted peg gives 2x bonus, re-picks on hit
  - Distance: fixed rings, focus far pegs
  - Trick Shot: 20 rings, track special tricks
  - Daily Challenge: 10 rings, date-seeded PRNG layout
  - Survival: 90/60/45s timer, 3 misses = game over
  - Practice: unlimited, no pressure
- 3 difficulty levels: Easy/Medium/Hard affecting ring count, timer duration
- Combo scoring: consecutive ringers build multiplier x1 to x10, 2.5s decay timer, points = base * min(combo, 10)
- 40 achievements with localStorage:
  - Ringer milestones (1/10/50/100/500), score thresholds (500/1K/5K/10K), combo tiers (3/5/8/10)
  - Golden ringer, double ringer, bounce ringer, accuracy (80%/100%), perfect game

This is the midnight kick-off job. You start a fresh IWSDK game build from scratch.

### Status file protocol:

You MUST maintain `~/workspace/iwsdk-daily-builds/current-build-status.json` throughout.

**At the start**, write:
```json
{
```

**When your build round ends**, update the status file:
- Set `status` to `"waiting_continuation"` (if under 6h) or `"complete"` (if ≥6h)
- Append to `rounds` array: `{"round": N, "start_utc": "...", "end_utc": "...", "minutes": N, "files": N, "lines": N, "features_added": [...]}`

### ⚠️ CRITICAL: Spatial UI Only — NO HTML Overlays

**ALL game UI MUST use IWSDK's built-in PanelUI system. Do NOT use HTML DOM elements for any game UI.**

This is a hard gate. HTML `<div>`, `<canvas>`, `document.createElement`, `innerHTML`, or any DOM overlay for menus, HUDs, scorecards, settings, notifications, or any other game UI is **forbidden**. HTML overlays are invisible in XR and are an anti-pattern.

Instead, use:
- **`.uikitml` templates** in a `ui/` directory, compiled by `@iwsdk/vite-plugin-uikitml`
- **`PanelUI` component** to attach compiled UI panels to entities
- **`Follower` component** with `world.player.head` target for head-locked HUDs in XR
- **`ScreenSpace` component** for browser-mode overlays that auto-return to world-space in XR
- **World-space panels** for in-scene menus, leaderboards, settings boards

Read the IWSDK dev skill section **4b** for full API details, examples, and patterns.

### ⚠️ CRITICAL: XR Verification Gate

**You MUST verify all UI and interactions work in XR BEFORE expanding features or adding content.**

Build order for every game:
1. Core gameplay loop + basic XR controller input
2. All UI as PanelUI spatial panels (menus, HUD, scorecards, settings)
3. **VERIFY in XR:** Use IWSDK CLI tools (`npx iwsdk xr`, `npx iwsdk ecs pause/step/snapshot`) to confirm:
   - All panels render and are readable in XR
   - XR controller laser pointer can interact with all buttons/menus
   - HUD panels follow the player's head correctly
   - No HTML overlays remain
4. ONLY THEN expand with additional features, content, modes, polish

If XR verification fails, fix the issues before adding anything else.

### Build instructions:

1. **Research and brainstorm** a new game concept. Be creative.

2. **Build it** in `~/workspace/<game-name>/`:
   - Use the latest IWSDK (currently 0.4.1+)
   - Holodeck aesthetic (clean, futuristic, neon wireframe, luminous)
   - **ALL UI via PanelUI** — `.uikitml` templates, `Follower` for HUDs, `ScreenSpace` for overlays. Zero HTML DOM UI.
   - **XR controller support is mandatory** — trigger to fire/interact, grip for grab, pointer for aiming/menus. Must work end-to-end with VR controllers only. Use IWSDK's InputComponent API and action system.
   - Support both VR AND browser-first mode with dual runtime (`xr: { offer: 'once' }` + `browserControls: true`)
   - Include audio (procedural sound effects, music)
   - Full gameplay loop with scoring, progression, polish
